newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - HK stocks seen pausing after firm start.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - HK stocks seen pausing after firm start.

text.p: Stocks are likely to take a breather in the week ahead after their recent ascent, but only after the surprisingly weak U.S. September jobs report has provided an early fillip to Hang Seng index, analysts said.

On Friday, the U.S. Commerce Department reported that non-farm payrolls fell by 40,000 in September compared to an expected rise of 166,000. This quelled fears of higher interest rates, and stocks on Wall Street rallied. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 60.01 points to a record close of 5,992.86 and the U.S. long bond added 1-3/32 to yield 6.75 percent, the lowest closing yield since August 12.

"The (Hong Kong) market is due for a correction, but this type of news will have the opposite effect and keep people fully invested," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.
"This is the type of data that can bring the market back above the 12,000 mark, but somewhere along the line there is going to be some sort of correction, albeit minor perhaps," he added.

"Hong Kong does need a consolidation, but there is not a lot that will bring us into a consolidation -- there is plenty of momentum buying, and volume has held up very well. These are indications of a bullish market," added Rossiter.

The Hang Seng index powered through resistance at 12,000 points last week, closing above that mark on Thursday at 12,014.56, the first time since February 1994. It fell 109.05 points on Friday to 11,905.51, but despite that loss the index gained 146 points, or 1.24 percent, over the week.
After Friday's close in Hong Kong, the U.S. jobs data propelled Hong Kong stocks higher in London, with the Hang Seng London Reference index advancing 124.48 points to 12,029.99.

"We have moved up very strongly and any consolidation would be healthy to provide a base for a trading range or a platform for a move up," said Miles Remington, sales trader at Crosby Securities. "There is still a belief that there is further upside -- it is just a question of how quickly we can attain the 12,000 level and move through that resistance."
Analysts said the recent pick-up in turnover and confidence about the corporate earnings outlook would minimise the impact of a market pullback.

"I think funds will continue to come into the market," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International. "I don't think the market is going to see a major correction...(there may be) some profit-taking (but the market) will stay quite firm."
He noted that there had been a revival in H-shares, or those of China-incorporated companies listed in Hong Kong.
"H-shares used to be market laggards; now they are picking up. There is renewed buying interest in H-shares after red chips moved higher in recent weeks," Tang said.
Red chips are big-capital stocks listed in Hong Kong that have major backing from China.
"We have seen the China factor become increasingly positive. More and more fund managers are of the opinion that the China factor will play a major role," he said.
